h.strategy: Use retrieved findings to classify settings as strong, weak, neutral or harmful, and to identify which settings can disconnect other parts from the outcome. Propose hypotheses only of two kinds. Self-conditioning: the edit's effect depends on the value it replaces, being more negative when that value is strong and more positive when it is empty or harmful. Disconnection: when the edited part cannot influence the outcome, its effect shrinks toward zero, so the direction is lower if the edit usually helps and higher if it usually hurts. Directions refer to the signed effect. For each hypothesis, state the edit's usual sign and a one-sentence mechanism. Cover varied edit fields and values. The critic should replace any hypothesis with an uncertain usual sign, competing effects or reliance on partial redundancy.

hyps.why: With edge 0 removed node 1 has no input so edge 4 carries nothing and the usual conv gain shrinks toward zero.
Node 2 exits only via edge 5, so with edge 5 removed edge 2 is disconnected and the gain vanishes.
Edge 1 feeds only node 2 whose sole exit is edge 5, so with edge 5 removed the edit cannot reach the output.
With edge 0 removed node 1 receives no input so edge 2 carries nothing and adding a conv there gains almost nothing.
With edge 5 removed edge 1 is already dead, so deleting it is harmless whereas deleting a live edge normally hurts.
Replacing an empty direct edge with a conv adds a whole new path, a larger gain than when edge 3 already carries a useful op.
Filling an empty final edge restores the node-2 route to the output, giving a bigger gain than upgrading an existing op.
Downgrading a strong 3x3 conv hurts, so the signed effect is more negative than when the replaced op was already weak or absent.
Swapping a 3x3 conv for a parameter-free skip loses more than swapping in skip for a weak op or an empty edge.
Removing an edge hurts most when the removed op was a strong 3x3 conv.
